Calculate the percentage of parent decayed by dividing the radiogenic daughter by the initial parent, and multiplying by one hundred. Return a list containing the initial parent amount, the calculated age, the error estimate, and the percentage decayed. Example: given fifty parent moles, thirty daughter moles, and a half life of seven hundred, output the dating results.

title: Timber Cruise Volume
spec: Calculates the merchantable timber volume of a forest stand given a list of tree counts per plot, average diameter at breast height in inches, and usable height in feet. The entry function `timber(counts, diameter, height)` determines the total number of trees by summing the plot counts in the list. Calculate the average plot density by dividing the total number of trees by the number of plots. Compute the basal area per tree in square feet by squaring the diameter, then multiplying by zero point zero zero five four five four. Multiply the basal area by the usable height to get the cylindrical volume. Apply a form class taper factor of zero point seven eight to find the cubic foot volume per tree. Convert the cubic foot volume to board feet by multiplying by twelve and applying a sawkerf loss factor of zero point six. Multiply the board foot volume per tree by the total number of trees to find the total stand volume. Estimate the defect deduction by multiplying the total stand volume by zero point zero five. Calculate the net merchantable volume by subtracting the defect deduction from the total stand volume. Return a list containing the total tree count, the board foot volume per tree, and the net merchantable volume. Example: given counts of five, eight, and six, a diameter of fourteen, and a height of thirty two, return the volume metrics.

title: Photogrammetric Scale Calculator
spec: Calculates aerial photography mapping parameters given the flying height in meters above sea level, the camera focal length in millimeters, and the average terrain elevation in meters. The entry function `scale(height, focal, elevation)` converts the focal length to meters by dividing by one thousand. Calculate the relative flying height by subtracting the terrain elevation from the flying height. Compute the photo scale factor by dividing the relative flying height by the focal length. The resulting photo scale is one divided by this factor. Next, determine the ground coverage of a standard aerial photo by setting the sensor width and height to zero point two three meters each. Multiply the sensor width by the scale factor to find the ground width in meters. Multiply the sensor height by the scale factor to find the ground height in meters. Calculate the total footprint area in square kilometers by multiplying the ground width by the ground height, then dividing by one million. Compute the required image spacing for a sixty percent forward overlap by multiplying the ground height by zero point four. Return a list containing the scale factor, the footprint area, and the forward image spacing. Example: given a height of three thousand, focal length of one hundred fifty, and elevation of five hundred, return the mapping parameters.

title: Pump Cavitation Risk
spec: Evaluates the net positive suction head available for a water pump given its elevation above sea level in meters, the water temperature in Celsius, and the friction loss in the suction pipe in meters. The entry function `npsh(elevation, temperature, friction)` calculates the atmospheric pressure head in meters of water starting with standard sea level pressure head of ten point three three meters, and subtracting the elevation multiplied by zero point zero zero one two. Next, estimate the vapor pressure head of the water by dividing the temperature by one hundred, squaring the result, and multiplying by five point two. Calculate the static suction head by assuming the water source is two point five meters below the pump, resulting in a negative static head of two point five. Compute the total dynamic suction head by adding the static head and the friction loss. Calculate the available suction head by subtracting the vapor pressure head and the total dynamic suction head from the atmospheric pressure head. Apply a safety margin by subtracting an additional zero point five meters. Determine the critical cavitation parameter by dividing the available suction head by the total dynamic suction head. Return a list containing the atmospheric pressure head, the available suction head, and the critical parameter. Example: given an elevation of five hundred, temperature of twenty five, and friction of one point two, output the cavitation metrics.

title: Fiber Optic Dispersion
spec: Calculates the chromatic dispersion and modal bandwidth for a fiber optic link given the link length in kilometers, operating wavelength in nanometers, and zero dispersion slope in picoseconds per nanometer squared per kilometer. The entry function `dispersion(length, wavelength, slope)` assumes the zero dispersion wavelength is one thousand three hundred ten nanometers. Compute the wavelength difference by subtracting the zero dispersion wavelength from the operating wavelength. Calculate the dispersion coefficient by multiplying the zero dispersion slope by the operating wavelength, dividing by four, and multiplying by the result of one minus the fourth power of the zero dispersion wavelength divided by the operating wavelength. Multiply the dispersion coefficient by the link length to find the total chromatic dispersion in picoseconds per nanometer. Determine the spectral width of the light source, assumed to be two nanometers. Calculate the pulse spreading by multiplying the total dispersion by the spectral width. Estimate the modal bandwidth in megahertz kilometers by dividing four hundred forty by the pulse spreading. Calculate the total link bandwidth by dividing the modal bandwidth by the link length. Compute the bandwidth penalty by multiplying the pulse spreading by zero point zero five. Subtract this penalty from the total link bandwidth to get the effective bandwidth. Return a list containing the total dispersion, pulse spreading, and effective bandwidth. Example: given a length of forty, wavelength of one thousand five hundred fifty, and slope of zero point zero nine, return the metrics.

title: Cheese Maturation Yield
spec: Calculates the final cheese yield and composition over a maturation period given the initial milk weight in kilograms, milk fat percentage, and target moisture percentage. The entry function `cheese(milk, fat, moisture)` determines the fat mass by multiplying the milk weight by the fat percentage and dividing by one hundred. Calculate the casein mass by assuming the casein percentage is zero point seven eight times the fat percentage, then multiplying by the milk weight and dividing by one hundred. Compute the total solid non fat mass by multiplying the casein mass by one point zero nine. Calculate the initial curd weight by multiplying the sum of the fat and solid non fat masses by one point six. Determine the initial moisture mass in the curd by subtracting the fat and solid masses from the curd weight. During maturation, ten percent of the initial moisture evaporates. Calculate the lost moisture mass by multiplying the initial moisture by zero point one. Compute the final cheese weight by subtracting the lost moisture from the initial curd weight. Calculate the final actual moisture percentage by dividing the remaining moisture by the final cheese weight and multiplying by one hundred. Compute the yield percentage by dividing the final cheese weight by the milk weight and multiplying by one hundred. Return a list with the final cheese weight, final moisture percentage, and yield percentage. Example: given one thousand kilograms of milk, a fat percentage of three point five, and a target moisture of thirty five, output the maturation results.

title: Concrete Slab Deflection
spec: Calculates the maximum immediate deflection of a reinforced concrete slab given the span length in meters, uniform distributed load in kilonewtons per square meter, and slab thickness in millimeters. The entry function `deflection(span, load, thickness)` converts the thickness to meters by dividing by one thousand. Set the concrete elastic modulus to twenty five million kilonewtons per square meter. Consider a one meter wide strip of the slab. Calculate the gross moment of inertia by multiplying the width of one meter by the cube of the thickness, then dividing by twelve. Compute the maximum bending moment by multiplying the distributed load by the square of the span length, then dividing by eight. Set the cracking moment to the modulus of rupture, which is three thousand kilonewtons per square meter, multiplied by the gross moment of inertia, divided by half the thickness. Compute the effective moment of inertia: if the cracking moment exceeds the maximum moment, use the gross moment of inertia; otherwise, reduce the gross moment by multiplying it by the cube of the cracking moment divided by the maximum moment. Calculate the maximum deflection in meters by multiplying the load by five and the fourth power of the span, then dividing by three hundred eighty four times the elastic modulus times the effective moment of inertia. Convert the deflection to millimeters by multiplying by one thousand. Return a list containing the moment of inertia, maximum moment, and final deflection. Example: given a span of five, load of ten, and thickness of two hundred, return the parameters.

title: Centrifugal Compressor Surge
spec: Evaluates the operating point of a centrifugal compressor relative to its surge line. The entry function `surge(flow, speed, pressure)` takes the inlet mass flow rate in kilograms per second, rotational speed in revolutions per minute, and discharge pressure in kilopascals. First, establish the baseline inlet pressure as one hundred one kilopascals. Compute the pressure ratio by dividing the discharge pressure by the inlet pressure. Calculate the corrected speed by dividing the rotational speed by the square root of a reference temperature of two hundred ninety eight kelvin. Determine the surge margin flow by multiplying the corrected speed by zero point zero zero one five and adding zero point five. Next, compute the actual corrected mass flow by dividing the mass flow by the square root of the reference temperature. Calculate the surge flow deviation by subtracting the surge margin flow from the actual corrected flow. Determine the surge pressure limit by multiplying the actual corrected flow by two point five and adding one point zero. Calculate the pressure deviation by subtracting the surge pressure limit from the pressure ratio. Calculate a safety metric by dividing the surge flow deviation by the surge margin flow and multiplying by one hundred. Return a list containing the corrected flow, pressure ratio, and the safety metric percentage. Example: given a flow of two, speed of ten thousand, and pressure of three hundred, return the computed operational states.

title: Optical Fiber Power Budget
spec: Evaluates whether a fiber optic link will operate reliably given the transmit power in decibel milliwatts, total fiber distance in kilometers, and the number of fusion splices. The entry function `budget(power, distance, splices)` defines the receiver sensitivity threshold as negative twenty eight decibel milliwatts. Calculate the total fiber attenuation by multiplying the distance by the standard loss of zero point two five decibels per kilometer. Calculate the total splice loss by multiplying the number of splices by zero point one decibels. Include a connector loss at both ends by adding zero point seven five decibels twice. Add a system repair margin of three decibels to account for future degradation. Compute the total system loss by summing the fiber attenuation, total splice loss, connector losses, and the repair margin. Determine the received optical power by subtracting the total system loss from the transmit power. Calculate the link power margin by subtracting the receiver sensitivity threshold from the received optical power. Check the link viability; assign a value of one if the power margin is greater than zero, otherwise assign zero. Return a list with the total system loss, the received optical power, the link power margin, and the viability indicator. Example: given a transmit power of zero, distance of forty, and four splices, return the power budget analysis.

title: Turbine Blade Stress
spec: Calculates the centrifugal tensile stress at the root of a gas turbine blade given the blade tip radius in meters, the rotational speed in revolutions per minute, and the root cross sectional area in square meters. The entry function `stress(radius, speed, area)` sets the material density to eight thousand kilograms per cubic meter. Define the hub radius as zero point four meters. Compute the angular velocity in radians per second by multiplying the rotational speed by pi, then dividing by thirty. Calculate the blade length by subtracting the hub radius from the tip radius. Determine the center of mass radius by adding half the blade length to the hub radius. Compute the total mass of the blade by multiplying the density by the root area and the blade length. In reality blades taper, so apply a taper reduction factor of zero point six to the total mass. Calculate the centrifugal force by multiplying the tapered mass by the center of mass radius and the square of the angular velocity. Find the root stress in pascals by dividing the centrifugal force by the root area. Convert the stress to megapascals by dividing by one million. Calculate the safety factor by dividing the material yield strength of eight hundred megapascals by the computed root stress. Return a list containing the angular velocity, the centrifugal force, the stress in megapascals, and the safety factor. Example: given a tip radius of zero point eight, speed of three thousand, and root area of zero point zero zero five, return the stress metrics.

title: European Option Pricing
spec: Entry function `price(parameters)`. Input is a numeric vector of length five representing current asset price, strike price, risk free interest rate, volatility, and time to maturity in years. Calculate the intermediate mathematical terms for the standard pricing formula. Compute the normal cumulative distribution function values for these terms. Use these probabilities to calculate the final call option price and the put option price. Combine both final prices into a list. For example, given an input of one hundred, one hundred, zero point zero five, zero point two, and one, return a list with ten point four five and five point five seven.

title: Bond Yield Metrics
spec: Entry function `evaluate(bond)`. Input is a list containing face value, annual coupon rate, years to maturity, and current market price. Calculate the annual coupon payment amount. Use a discrete iterative approach to find the yield to maturity that equates the present value of all future cash flows to the market price. Calculate the present value of each cash flow using this yield. Determine the Macaulay duration by summing the time weighted present values and dividing by the market price. Return a numeric vector containing the calculated yield and the duration.

title: Multiplayer Rank Updater
spec: Entry function `update(results)`. Input is a numeric matrix where each row contains a player one rating, a player two rating, and a win indicator for player one. Iterate over each match row. Calculate the expected probability of winning for each player using the standard logistic rating curve formula. Calculate the rating change by multiplying a scaling factor of thirty two by the difference between the actual outcome and the expected outcome. Add the rating change to both players. Return a new matrix with the updated ratings for all matches.

title: Sensor Anomaly Detector
spec: Entry function `detect(readings)`. Input is a numeric vector of sequential sensor values. Iterate through the sequence using a rolling window of size five. For each window, extract the subset of five values. Calculate the statistical mean and standard deviation of this subset. Check if the center value of the window deviates by more than two standard deviations from the calculated mean. If it does, record the index of this center value. Return a numeric vector of all recorded anomalous indices.

title: Habitat Capacity Modeler
spec: Entry function `simulate(parameters)`. Input is a numeric vector containing the initial population size, the intrinsic growth rate, the environmental carrying capacity, and the number of generations to simulate. Set up a loop to simulate the population size generation by generation using the discrete logistic growth equation. In each step, calculate the new population and store it in a tracking vector. Identify the specific generation index where the population first strictly exceeds ninety percent of the carrying capacity. Return a list containing the final tracked population vector and this generation index.

title: Darts Leg Scorer
spec: Entry function `score(throws)`. Input is a list of plain text strings representing darts thrown in a single game of five hundred and one. The strings use words like twenty, double ten, or outer bull. Iterate over each throw and convert the text into its corresponding numerical value. Subtract this numerical value from the running total score. If a throw causes the remaining score to reach exactly one or drop below zero, mark that throw and all subsequent ones as invalid. Return a list containing the final remaining score and the count of valid throws.

title: Damped Oscillator Modeler
spec: Entry function `simulate(conditions)`. Input is a list containing the object mass, spring constant, damping coefficient, initial displacement, and a small time step increment. Initialize the position, velocity, and time variables. Run a numerical integration loop for two hundred time steps. In each iteration, calculate the current acceleration based on the spring force and damping resistance. Update the velocity and then the position. Keep track of the absolute displacements. Return the maximum absolute displacement observed during the entire simulation.

title: Term Importance Extractor
spec: Entry function `extract(documents)`. Input is a list of three plain text sentences. Split each sentence into individual lowercase words to build a vocabulary. For each sentence, count the frequency of each word. Calculate the inverse document frequency for every word across the three sentences. Multiply the word frequencies by their respective inverse document frequencies to calculate the importance scores. Identify the highest score achieved by any word in the entire set. Return this maximum numeric score.

title: Cluster Center Initializer
spec: Entry function `initialize(points)`. Input is a two column numeric matrix of spatial coordinates. Select the first row as the first cluster center and store it. To find the next three centers, iterate through all remaining points. Calculate the Euclidean distance from each point to all currently stored centers. Find the minimum distance for each point. Select the point that has the maximum of these minimum distances and add it to the stored centers. Repeat until four centers are found. Return a matrix of the chosen coordinates.

title: Protein Charge Calculator
spec: Entry function `charge(sequence)`. Input is a single text string of uppercase amino acid letters. Split the string into individual characters. Count the total number of basic residues like lysine, arginine, and histidine. Count the acidic residues like aspartic acid and glutamic acid. Use standard acid dissociation constant formulas to calculate the partial charge of each group at a physiological baseline of seven point four. Sum the positive and negative contributions. Return the net numeric charge of the sequence.

title: Relative Strength Index
spec: Entry function `calculate(prices)`. Input is a numeric vector of consecutive daily closing prices. Iterate through the vector to compute the day to day price changes. Separate these changes into positive gains and absolute negative losses. Calculate the initial average gain and average loss over a rolling fourteen day period. Use a smoothed moving average for the subsequent days to update the average gains and losses. Compute the relative strength ratio and the final index value for each day. Return a numeric vector of the index.

title: Photon Scattering Simulator
spec: Entry function `scatter(photons)`. Input is a numeric integer representing the number of particles entering a medium. For each particle, start at an initial position of zero. Use a random number generator to determine the distance traveled before a scattering event based on an absorption coefficient. Calculate a random scattering angle and update the horizontal and vertical coordinates. Continue stepping until the particle either exceeds a specified depth or returns past the entry point. Count how many particles successfully cross the depth threshold. Return this count.

title: Network Connection Minimizer
spec: Entry function `connect(matrix)`. Input is a symmetric numeric matrix representing the cost of connecting various nodes, with zeros on the diagonal. Create a list of visited nodes starting with the first index, and a list of unvisited nodes containing the rest. Set a running total cost to zero. Iteratively search the matrix to find the lowest non zero cost connecting any node in the visited list to any node in the unvisited list. Add this cost to the total and move the identified node to the visited list. Return the final total cost.

title: String Edit Distance
spec: Entry function `distance(words)`. Input is a list containing two plain text strings. Determine the length of both strings. Create a numeric matrix with rows equal to the first length plus one and columns equal to the second length plus one. Fill the first row and first column with sequential integers starting from zero. Iterate through the remaining cells, calculating the cost of inserting, deleting, or substituting a character by looking at the adjacent matrix values. Return the final integer cost located in the bottom right cell.

title: Sequence Transition Modeler
spec: Entry function `generate(sequence)`. Input is a list of sequential words. Iterate through the list to extract all consecutive pairs of words. Count the occurrences of each pair to build a frequency table of transitions from a current word to a next word. Convert these frequency counts into transition probabilities. Starting with the very first word of the input, use the probabilities to randomly select a subsequent word. Repeat this process to build a new sequence of exactly ten words. Return the new sequence as a single string.

title: Logic Grid Validator
spec: Entry function `validate(grid)`. Input is a nine by nine numeric matrix representing a completed number puzzle. Check the matrix to ensure it contains only integers from one to nine. Iterate over every row and verify that it contains exactly nine unique numbers. Iterate over every column to verify the same condition. Divide the grid into nine separate three by three blocks and check each block for uniqueness. If any check fails, immediately store a false status. Return a single boolean indicating if all rules are satisfied.

title: Color Space Converter
spec: Entry function `convert(pixels)`. Input is a matrix with three columns representing red, green, and blue intensities from zero to two hundred fifty five. Divide all values by two hundred fifty five to normalize them. For each row, identify the maximum and minimum values among the three channels. Calculate the lightness as the average of the maximum and minimum. Calculate the saturation based on the difference between the maximum and minimum. Determine the hue angle based on which color channel is the maximum. Return a new matrix of the converted values.

title: Spatial Image Filter
spec: Entry function `filter(image)`. Input is a numeric matrix representing grayscale pixel values. Define a three by three edge detection matrix containing specific positive and negative weights. Create an output matrix of the same dimensions filled with zeros. Iterate over the inner pixels of the input matrix, avoiding the outer border. Extract the local three by three neighborhood for each pixel. Multiply the neighborhood by the detection matrix, sum all the values, and store the result in the output matrix. Return the new filtered matrix.

title: Bridge Thermal Expansion
spec: Entry function `expand(temperatures)`. Input is a numeric vector of daily ambient temperatures in Celsius. Define a starting bridge length of one thousand meters and a standard thermal expansion coefficient. Iterate through the temperature readings. Calculate the temperature difference from a twenty degree baseline for each day. Calculate the linear expansion or contraction using the coefficient and the starting length. Update the daily length of the structure. Identify and store the maximum overall length and the maximum single day change. Return a list containing these two values.

title: Atmospheric Refraction Modeler
spec: Entry function `refract(angles)`. Input is a numeric vector of initial celestial observation angles in degrees. Iterate through each angle to apply a standard atmospheric refraction formula. Calculate a correction factor based on standard sea level temperature and pressure. Convert the initial degree angle into radians for trigonometric calculations. Compute the tangent of the angle and use it to find the refraction adjustment in arcminutes. Convert the adjustment back to degrees and subtract it from the initial angle. Return the numeric vector of true angles.

title: Fractal Dimension Estimator
spec: Entry function `estimate(grid)`. Input is a two dimensional numeric matrix consisting entirely of zeros and ones. Start with a block size equal to the matrix width. Count how many square blocks of this size contain at least one positive value. Divide the block size by two and repeat the counting process across the partitioned grid. Continue dividing and counting until the block size reaches a width of one. Calculate the natural logarithm of the sizes and the counts. Perform a linear regression and return the numeric slope of the line.

title: Symbol Compression Tree
spec: Entry function `build(text)`. Input is a plain text string. Split the string and count the frequency of each unique character. Create a list where each element represents a node with a character and its frequency. Start a loop that continues until only one node remains in the list. Inside the loop, identify the two nodes with the lowest frequencies. Create a new combined node whose frequency is the sum of the two. Remove the original two nodes and add the combined one back to the list. Return the final root frequency.

title: Mahalanobis Distance Calculator
spec: Entry function `mahalanobis(data)`. Input is a numeric matrix where rows represent samples and columns represent features. Calculate the arithmetic mean of each column. Create a new matrix by subtracting the respective column mean from every row. Calculate the covariance matrix by multiplying the transposed centered matrix by itself and dividing by the number of rows. Compute the mathematical inverse of this covariance matrix. For each row in the centered matrix, calculate the specific distance by multiplying the row by the inverse and then by the transposed row. Return the numeric distances.
